props.title: Odd Man Out
props.initialSlug: Wounded IRA leader flees through nighttime Belfast

sections.content: Odd Man Out (1947) stands as Carol Reed's masterful noir thriller about an IRA leader's desperate final hours in Belfast. James Mason delivers a haunting performance as Johnny McQueen, wounded after a robbery gone wrong and stumbling through shadowy streets as both police and compatriots hunt him. The film's expressionistic style echoes The Third Man (1949), Reed's later masterpiece, but here the darkness feels even more suffocating. Like The Informer (1935), it transforms Ireland's political struggles into pure noir atmosphere, but Reed's vision is uniquely poetic and fatalistic.

sections.content: Reed's direction creates a dreamlike descent into darkness, with Johnny's journey becoming increasingly surreal as night falls. The film shares DNA with French poetic realism like Le Jour Se Lève (1939), where doomed protagonists face inevitable fate in stylized urban settings. The supporting characters - artists, criminals, priests - form a grotesque gallery reminiscent of The Face of Another (1966), each reflecting different aspects of Johnny's fragmenting psyche.

The film's influence echoes through later political thrillers, particularly in its treatment of urban warfare and moral ambiguity. The Battle of Algiers (1966) shares its documentary-like attention to resistance movements, while Cal (1984) directly references its portrayal of Northern Ireland's conflicts. But Reed's focus remains intensely personal rather than political, using expressionist techniques to convey psychological torment. SUBHEAD: Visual Innovation and Legacy

sections.content: Reed and cinematographer Robert Krasker developed revolutionary techniques to capture Belfast's rain-slicked streets and looming shadows. Their canted angles and deep focus photography influenced film noir globally, visible in everything from Night and the City (1950) to Touch of Evil (1958). The film's climactic scenes in an artist's studio, with their hallucinatory quality, prefigure the psychological horror of Repulsion (1965) and the urban alienation of Taxi Driver (1976).
